# The Heat Is Unequal: How Cities Can Make Summer Bearable

Summer in the city has always been hotter than summer in the countryside, but climate change has transformed a familiar discomfort into a genuine public health crisis. Urban heat islands—the phenomenon whereby cities run several degrees hotter than surrounding areas—now kill more Americans in a typical year than hurricanes, floods, and tornadoes combined. The 2021 heat dome over the Pacific Northwest, which killed hundreds of people in Portland, Seattle, and Vancouver, demonstrated that even cities historically unaccustomed to extreme heat can become lethal. The question is no longer whether cities should adapt to heat, but how. The answer involves trees, street design, housing, and transit, and it requires confronting an uncomfortable truth: the burden of urban heat falls hardest on those least able to escape it.

## The Problem of the Heat Island

Cities are hot by design. Asphalt and concrete absorb solar radiation during the day and release it slowly at night, preventing the cooling that rural areas enjoy. Cars, air conditioners, and industry pump waste heat into the streets. Tall buildings block breezes and trap warm air.
